newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says Germany to stick to strict EMU goals.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says Germany to stick to strict EMU goals.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday recent economic data would not force Germany to abandon its budget forecasts and Bonn would still meet the fiscal targets for European monetary union.

Should economic developments endanger Germany's ability to meet the Maastricht treaty targets, Waigel said Bonn would not hesitate to take additional measures to rein in budget deficits and called for strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.
"I have not changed my view. I will oppose any weakening of the criteria, three is three," Waigel said in the text of a speech prepared for delivery in Ludwigsburg.
Waigel said he was responding to recent speculation that Germany was considering a looser interpretation of the criteria for monetary union.
"Convergence will determine the timetable -- for each country," he said.
The treaty on European economic and monetary union states that participants must fulfil a range of fiscal targets in 1997 and demonstrate lasting fiscal stability.
Based on economic data from this year, the European Union will determine early next year which countries meet the targets and qualify for entry into monetary union in 1999.

While most countries already meet some of the targets such as inflation below three percent, most are having difficulties meeting the cap on public debt of 60 percent of gross domestic product and on budget deficits of three percent of GDP.
Germany failed last year to meet the targets and runs the risk of missing the goals again this year.
This has fuelled speculation that either EMU will begin with weaker criteria or it will have to be delayed because it would be unthinkable without Germany or France.

"The yardstick is the lasting fulfilment of the determined criteria. The German government considers it indispensable that there is a strict and narrow interpretation of the treaty regulations at the time of the examination of convergence," Waigel said.

"Germany will fulfil the criteria," he added. "Even current developments give no cause to veer from these forecasts. But should there still be a need to act, we will not hesitate to do what is necessary."

Waigel also took time to explain that Germany's austerity measures were not only aimed at meeting the Maastricht targets, but that budget savings were needed to get Europe's biggest economy back in shape for global competition.
But without the timely introduction of the euro, as the new currency will be called, market pressures could develop that could wipe out the progress that Germany has made in this direction.
"If the euro does not come, the mark will come under upward pressure. The export economy will suffer, jobs will be lost and public budgets will be hit," Waigel warned.
"Monetary union is our deepest interest. The export nation Germany will benefit from open markets without exchange rate risks, from a strong, stable euro bloc in the world monetary system."
